title: Teacher Credibility
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart presents Teacher Credibility as the foundational belief of his Five Key Beliefs framework, citing John Hattie's finding that Teacher Credibility has a massive effect size in education research. He argues teachers are constantly sending Credibility signals, whether intentional or not, and reduces the signal categories to three: Care, Competence, and Passion. From there he narrows a long list of possible interventions down to three core strategies, Tracking MGCs, Improve at One Thing, and Gentle Urgency, and provides a lengthy FAQ addressing common teacher anxieties: undermining one's own credibility, working alongside a weak colleague, feeling incompetent as a new teacher, disliking one's own curriculum, and recovering from a rocky start to the year.
points: Stuart's cell-tower analogy captures his central claim: teachers are always sending signals to students whether they intend to or not, and those signals accumulate into a Credibility verdict in students' minds.
The CCP framework (Care, Competence, Passion) compresses a complex research literature into a simple self-assessment tool teachers can revisit periodically.

His advice for teachers who dislike their assigned curriculum splits the problem into personal versus professional distaste and recommends extra research outside intra-disciplinary echo chambers before settling professional views in stone.
He reassures teachers that first-week missteps are recoverable because Credibility is mostly built in the humdrum of daily encounters, not a one-shot first impression.
quotes: Teachers are like cell phone towers. A cell tower is always sending signals, whether my cell phone is on or off. That is the cell tower's job.
In terms of Credibility, I am always sending signals to my students, whether I want to or not.
In the largest meta-analytical research effort ever undertaken in education, researcher John Hattie finds that Teacher Credibility has a massive effect size.
I do not recommend trying to convince your students that you are Credible. Instead, show them you are Credible by consistently signaling Care, Competence, and Passion.
So do some extra research, particularly outside of intra-disciplinary echo chambers, before you set your professional views in stone. It'll make the job a lot more fun and interesting.
In other words, while it's true that first days have special characteristics in the hearts of our students, it's mostly in the humdrum where Credibility is made or lost.
